choices.C: The form's submit button was labeled "Log In" instead of "Sign In," which is a subtle phishing indicator detectable by a trained user.
choices.D: The browser displayed the correct favicon (site icon) for the banking portal, which proves the page is genuine and the "Not Secure" warning is a false positive.

items.explanation: The URL bar and padlock icon (or its absence) are the browser's primary security indicators, visible before any interaction with the page content. When a user types https:// and the resulting page shows http:// in the URL bar with no padlock, this is the definitive visual indicator that TLS was not established, occurring at page load, before the form is rendered, before any credentials are entered. H1 confirms this: the URL shows HTTP and the browser explicitly warns "No padlock icon, browser downgraded to HTTP." This indicator is always present and requires no page inspection skills to notice, only the habit of verifying the protocol indicator before entering credentials.

rationale.A: Page layout similarity is not a reliable security indicator, SSL stripping attacks serve the actual content from the real server (often via a relay), making the page visually identical to the legitimate site. Phishing sites also increasingly use cloned page designs. Visual similarity cannot confirm or deny legitimacy.
rationale.C: Button label variation is not a documented security indicator and is easily matched by an attacker who clones the page precisely. Relying on minor text variations requires the user to memorize exact page wording, not a scalable security practice.
rationale.D: Favicons are embedded in page HTML and are served by whoever controls the connection, in this case, the attacker's relay at 10.0.1.44, which can serve the real favicon by fetching it from the legitimate server. Favicons provide zero authentication value and cannot confirm page legitimacy.

items.stem: The attack chain required three enabling conditions: (1) DNS cache was poisonable (no DNSSEC); (2) the banking portal accepted HTTP connections (no HTTPS-only enforcement); (3) the browser did not enforce HTTPS (no HSTS preload for the domain). Which server-side and network-side control combination makes SSL stripping attacks against this banking portal impossible, regardless of whether the client's DNS cache is poisoned?

choices.A: Implement HTTP Strict Transport Security (HSTS) with a long max-age and "includeSubDomains" on the banking portal server, and submit the domain to browser HSTS preload lists, once the browser has stored the HSTS policy, it will refuse to load any HTTP version of the domain and will not follow HTTP redirects, making SSL stripping impossible even if DNS is poisoned and the attacker redirects traffic to their host.
choices.B: Require employees to manually type https:// before every login and train them to verify the padlock before entering credentials.
choices.C: Deploy a web application firewall (WAF) in front of the banking portal that blocks all HTTP connections from external sources, forcing users to connect via HTTPS.
choices.D: Issue TLS client certificates to all employees so the banking portal only accepts authenticated certificate-bearing connections, preventing the attacker from impersonating the portal.

items.explanation: HSTS (HTTP Strict Transport Security) is the specific countermeasure for SSL stripping. When a browser receives an HSTS header from banking.clearpath-internal.net, it stores a rule that all future connections to that domain must use HTTPS, the browser refuses to load HTTP and refuses to follow HTTP redirects for that domain, regardless of what an intermediate host (10.0.1.44) instructs. Even if DNS poisoning redirects to the attacker's IP, the browser's HSTS policy prevents it from accepting the HTTP 302 redirect. HSTS preloading extends this to browsers that have never visited the domain by including the domain in a built-in browser list. This makes SSL stripping impossible without also compromising the browser itself.

rationale.B: User training to manually type https:// does not prevent SSL stripping because the attack intercepts the HTTPS connection after the browser initiates it and redirects to HTTP before TLS is negotiated. H2 shows the browser sent a TLS ClientHello (correctly attempting HTTPS) and the attacker converted it to HTTP, the user's typing behavior was already correct. HSTS enforces the policy at the browser level without relying on user action.
rationale.C: A WAF blocking HTTP from external sources only applies to traffic that reaches the WAF. In this attack, the traffic never reaches the real server, it is redirected to 10.0.1.44 by DNS poisoning. The WAF has no visibility into the attacker's relay and cannot enforce HTTPS on connections that bypass the real server entirely.
rationale.D: TLS client certificates authenticate the client to the server, they would prevent unauthorized clients from accessing the real banking portal. However, in this attack, the attacker intercepts the connection before it reaches the real server. Client certificates do not prevent SSL stripping because the TLS handshake with the real server is replaced by the attacker's HTTP redirect before any certificate exchange. HSTS prevents the HTTP redirect from being accepted by the client browser.
